Autoantibodies to GABAergic neurons 
and response to plasmapheresis 
in stiff-man syndrome 
H. Robert Brashear, MD, and Lawrence H. Phillips 11, MD 
~ 
Article abstract-Stiff-man syndrome is a rare disorder of unknown etiology in which progressive rigidity, spasms, and 
continuous motor unit activity may be due to dysfunction of GABAergic inhibition of alpha motor neurons. Some patients with 
this disorder have evidence of autoantibodies reactive with glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). We describe a patient with 
progressive stiff-man syndrome and high titers of GAD-like immunoreactivity in serum but not spinal fluid. Plasmapheresis 
resulted in lowered antibody titers, decreased exteroceptive reflex responses, reduced motor unit activity, and marked clinical 
improvement. Immunohistochemistry using patient serum and plasma produced specific labeling of human and experimental 
animal tissue consistent with GABAergic neurons and terminal fields. This antibody response was not present in samples from 
more than 200 other patients. These results provide additional evidence of an autoimmune mechanism for stiff-man syndrome 
and indicate plasmapheresis may be beneficial in some patients. 
NEUROLOGY 1991;41:1588-1592 
Stiff-man syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by pro- 
gressive muscle rigidity and intermittent Muscle 
stiffness begins insidiously and progressively affects 
axial and proximal musculature, typically resulting in 
hyperlordosis and abnormal gait. Painful muscle 
spasms may dominate the clinical presentation and are 
often exacerbated by emotional and external stimuli. 
Neurologic examination usually reveals no other abnor- 
malities. EMG studies uniformly show continuous 
motor unit activity in affected muscles. A stereotypical 
reflex response to peripheral nerve stimulation has been 
de~cribed.~ Reflex discharges, referred to as "exterocep- 
tive" for their resemblance to the flexion reflex response 
to noxious stimulation, occur in muscles throughout the 
body after short trains of nonpainful stimuli. 
The etiology of stiff-man syndrome is unknown. The 
disorder responds to treatment with diazepam, which 
markedly diminishes continuous motor unit a~tivity"~.~ 
and exteroceptive reflex  response^.^ Ba~lofen,~.~ valpro- 
ate,g and clonazepam1° have also been effective in treat- 
ment. This and other clinical evidence support the 
hypothesis that stiff-man syndrome results from an 
imbalance between inhibitory input utilizing gamma- 
aminobutyric acid (GABA) and excitatory input to al- 
pha motor neurons.sJ1 Solimena et all2 presented evi- 
dence that serum and CSF autoantibodies in a patient 
with stiff -man syndrome, seizures, and diabetes melli- 
tus reacted with glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), 
the synthesizing enzyme for GABA, which is specifi- 
cally localized in GABAergic neurons. Subsequently, 
these authors described similar autoantibodies in 19 
additional patients diagnosed as having stiff-man syn- 
drome.13 Brief reports indicate the original patient im- 
proved clinically after pla~mapheresis'~; however, two 
other patients did We report a patient with pro- 
gressive stiff-man syndrome who had high titers of 
GAD-like immunoreactivity in serum but not CSF. She 
showed clinical and electrophysiologic improvement 
with plasmapheresis, which lowered antibody titers. 
Case report. A 37-year-old woman noted persistent low back 
pain following a minor motor vehicle accident in 1982. Evalua-

tion revealed mild scoliosis and kyphosis without other abnor- 
malities. Stiffness of gait and low back muscle spasms progres- 
sively worsened, leading to several falls. CT of the head, 
myelography, and CSF analysis were unremarkable. She was 
felt to have post-traumatic stress syndrome. The patient was 
treated with butalbital for pain and diazepam and baclofen for 
muscle spasms. As symptoms worsened, numerous other med- 
ications were tried. Diazepam resulted in the greatest im- 
provement and was slowly increased to 110 mg daily by 1986. 
In March 1989, she was taking 120 mg diazepam and 140 mg 
baclofen per day. She suffered a prolonged episode of severe 
lordotic spasms and was referred to the hospital. 
Examination revealed extensive vitiligo. There was pro- 
nounced rigidity and tenderness of axial muscles, with marked 
lordosis. She could walk with assistance, but the gait was rigid 
and slow. Her movements were often interrupted by painful

spasms of paraspinal and limb girdle muscles. Neck extension 
and rotation were severely limited. Strength, coordination, 
sensation, and deep tendon reflexes were normal, and plantar 
responses were flexor. Mental status and cranial nerve exami- 
nations were normal. We considered the diagnosis of stiff-man 
syndrome. EMG studies were normal except for continuous 
motor unit activity, mainly in the paraspinous muscles. Exag- 
gerated exteroceptive reflex responses were elicited. Both ex- 
teroceptive reflexes and continuous motor unit activity were 
abolished or markedly reduced following intravenous infusion 
of 10 mg diazepam, which did not produce any change in 
mental status. Radiographs of the spine showed marked lum- 
bar lordosis, and MRI was otherwise unremarkable. CSF anal- 
ysis was normal (protein, 28 mg/dl; IgG, 1.8 mg/dl; R value, 
0.56; and no oligoclonal bands). Metabolic screening, includ- 
ing random and fasting blood glucose levels, was normal. 
A trial of clonidine was initiated on the patient's discharge 
from the hospital, but was discontinued when she did not 
improve. Diazepam was increased to 130 mg daily, with mild 
reduction in spasms and rigidity. Indirect immunofluorescent 
screening of serum revealed autoantibody reactive with nor- 
mal human cerebellum in a pattern consistent with 
GABAergic terminals. The patient was readmitted to the 
hospital for a trial of plasmapheresis and consideration of 
immunosuppressive therapy. Serial antibody measurements, 
EMG studies, and plasmapheresis were carried out with her 
informed consent. 
Methods. Electrophysiologic techniques. Exteroceptive re- 
flexes were recorded using a modification of the technique 
described by Meinck et al.5 Surface recordings were made 
simultaneously from five muscle groups (abductor pollicis 
brevis, biceps brachii, lumbar paraspinal, biceps femoris, and 
tibialis anterior) using a TECA Mystro EMG. The recording 
gain was adjusted to obtain a well-defined signal from each 
channel. A frequency window of 20 Hz to 2,000 Hz was used in 
all recordings. The responses were full-wave-rectified and four 
responses were signal-averaged. Each response was obtained 
by delivering a train of five stimuli to the median nerve at the 
wrist at a rate of 200 Hz. The stimulus was delivered at the 
threshold for motor activation of the thenar muscles. 
Immunostaining. Aliquots of serum and CSF from routine 
laboratory studies were assayed against human, rat, and 
guinea pig tissue. Normal human brain tissue was obtained 
from autopsy cases within 4 hours of death, immediately 
frozen in liquid nitrogen-chilled isopentane, and preserved in 
the University of Virginia Brain Resource Facility. Cryostat 
sections were thaw-mounted, briefly fixed with acetone, and 
stored at -80 "C until use. Rat and guinea pig brain were 
treated similarly or were fixed by intracardiac perfusion with 
one of two fixatives: tissue for visualization of GABAergic 
terminals was fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate- 
buffered saline (PBS), and tissue for study of GABAergic cell 
bodies was perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde and 0.5% zinc 
salicylate in one-half normal saline.16 
Immunofluorescence was carried out on normal human 
brain sections as previously described.17 Serial twofold dilu- 
tions of serum and CSF were prepared with PBS and incu- 
bated with cryostat sections of normal tissue for 1 hour at 37 
"C. Sections were washed in PBS, overlaid with fluorescein-

conjugated rabbit antihuman IgG, IgA, IgE, or IgM for 1 hour 
at 37 "C, washed in PBS and distilled water, and examined 
with epifluorescent microscopy. Positive controls (sections 
incubated in dilutions of samples from patients with charac- 
terized antineuronal antibodies associated with para- 
neoplastic disorders) and negative controls (sections 
incubated in 1:40 normal human serum) were included with 
each series. Additional sections were incubated in 1:1,000 to 
2,000 dilutions of anti-GAD antibody'* (kindly provided by 
Dr. Donald Schmechel) for 4 hours, followed by fluorescein- 
conjugated rabbit antisheep IgG (Accurate). 
Immunoperoxidase staining was carried out on sections of 
fixed rat or guinea pig brain incubated in 1:160 to 1:1,280 
dilutions of patient serum overnight. After rinsing, sections 
were incubated in biotinylated antihuman IgG, reacted with 
avidin-biotin-peroxidase complex (ABC) (Vector), and devel- 
oped with diaminobenzidine. Adjacent sections were incu- 
bated in 1:2,000 to 4,000 anti-GAD antibody overnight, 
followed by biotinylated antisheep IgG (Vector), reacted with 
ABC, and developed with diaminobenzidine. Controls in- 
cluded assays with primary antibody omitted, and with bio- 
tinylated antibody directed against nonhuman or nonsheep 
IgG substituted for the appropriate secondary. 
Serial assessments during plasmapheresis. The patient 
underwent a course of five plasma exchanges of 2 liters each 
over 12 days. Medication dosages were unchanged during the 
month prior to admission and throughout plasmapheresis. 
Serum antibody titers were assayed on admission, after each 
plasma exchange, and on day 8 prior to the fourth plasma 
exchange. Endpoint titrations were read and ranked blindly. 
After completion of the course of plasmapheresis, all samples 
were assayed concurrently a second time by serial dilutions 
through endpoint staining against sections from the same 
block of tissue. Electrophysiologic studies were carried out on 
admission and after the first three plasma exchanges, as de- 
scribed above. Neurologic assessments were carried out daily 
by neurology staff and independently by one of us. In addition, 
the patient was asked to assess the degree of her rigidity, 
muscle spasms, and back pain. She rated each symptom on a 
10-point scale (10 being the worst, 1 being normal), and her 
responses were recorded twice each day. 
Results. Response to plasmapheresis. The patient tol- 
erated plasma exchange well, without complications. 
Serum titers of GAD-like immunoreactivity fell from 
1:1,280 to 1:80 during plasmapheresis. There was 
marked incremental improvement in EMG studies at 
each point tested. The areas of evoked exteroceptive 
reflex responses declined dramatically (figure 1). There 
was more than a fivefold decline in the size of the 
response in paraspinal muscles, from 26.2 to 4.98 pVsec, 
by the third plasma exchange (figure 2). Observed clini- 
cal response was equally striking: after two exchanges, 
rigidity had decreased, paraspinal muscles were palpa- 
bly less stiff, and the patient was able to sit up unas- 
sisted. During casual conversation, she turned her head 
to 90" in either direction. The patient reported mild 
improvement at this point. During the course of plas- 
mapheresis, her gait became progressively more fluid 
and she was able to walk without spasms. Subjective 
improvement fluctuated and lagged behind observed

measures but did not return to the preadmission state. 
Two weeks after discharge, she reported improvement 
to nearly normal functioning (a level of 2 on her 10-point 
scale, 1 being normal) and she had reduced diazepam 
dosage by 10 mg. 
Immunostaining. All samples of patient serum pro- 
duced bright, indirect immunofluorescent staining of 
sections of normal human brain (figure 3A). Immuno- 
fluorescent staining occurred only with fluorescein-la- 
beled antihuman IgG as the secondary antibody and not 
with anti-IgA, -IgE, or -IgM, or with anti-rabbit IgG. 
CSF did not produce staining, even when assayed un-

reflex responses measured over the course of 
plasmapheresis. Antibody titers are expressed as 
reciprocals. Exteroceptiue reflexes were measured over the 
paraspinal muscles at threshold median nerve stimulation. 
Triangles indicate days plasma exchanges were carried out. 
diluted. Sections read blindly for degree of staining were 
all ranked accurately by titrations. Endpoint titrations 
revealed persistent serum titers to 1:1,280 before plas- 
mapheresis and stepwise decline after plasma ex- 
changes. The same endpoints were determined when 
the assays were repeated concurrently. 
Serum produced a distinct punctate pattern of stain- 
ing specific for different brain regions and consistent 
with the known distribution of GABAergic termi- 
nals.16J9 Staining was particularly prominent in dorsal 
and ventral pallidum and in substantia nigra pars re- 
ticulata. Comparison of patient serum to anti-GAD 
immunostaining in adjacent brain sections from experi- 
mental animals showed the same distribution of stain- 
ing. Patient serum staining of rat spinal cord also 
matched anti-GAD staining,16 including labeling of 
punctate structures consistent with terminals on ante- 
rior horn cells. In tissue from animals perfused with a 
fixative protocol recommended by Mugnaini and Oertel 
to increase the staining of GAD-positive cell bodies,16 
the same distribution of immunoreactive neurons was 
seen with both anti-GAD and with patient serum stain- 
ing. 
This pattern of immunostaining was not seen in over 
200 serum and CSF samples from neurologically normal 
persons and from patients with a variety of neurologic 
disorders. Serum from only one other patient produced 
a punctate pattern of staining. This man had patholog- 
ically verified Alzheimer’s disease and marked para- 
tonia but no other movement disorder. His serum 
produced immunostaining of punctate and filamentous 
structures throughout the cortex, but labeling was dif- 
fuse and did not correspond to the known distribution 
of GABAergic terminals. Samples from two patients in 
whom the diagnosis of stiff-man syndrome was initially 
suspected but who had other causes of rigidity produced 
no staining. 
Discussion. This patient had classic findings of stiff- 
man syndrome. The response to plasmapheresis, car- 
ried out because of the presence of high serum titers of 
antibodies with GAD-like immunoreactivity, was strik- 
ing. Electrophysiologic and clinical improvement oc- 
curred within 6 hours after plasma exchange. This 
response underscores the potential reversibility of this 
disorder, consistent with the lack of neurologic deficits 
and of neuropathologic changes in most reported 
 case^.^^^ There was a longer delay in the patient’s subjec- 
tive improvement, which continued up to 2 weeks after 
plasmapheresis. Quantitation of exteroceptive reflex 
responses proved to be an excellent means of monitor- 
ing the course of therapy. Responses were abolished or 
markedly decreased with diazepam infusion, and de-

creasing responses paralleled the stepwise improve- 
ment in continuous motor unit activity, antibody titers, 
and clinical status during plasmapheresis. 
All serum samples produced labeling of neural struc- 
tures in a pattern consistent with anti-GAD antibody. 
Staining produced by patient serum matched not only 
anti-GAD labeling of terminals in adjacent sections, but 
also of GABAergic cell bodies when different methods 
of fixation were used. Antibody was of IgG class and 
reacted similarly with tissue from different species. 
This confirms the findings of Solimena et al,13 who have 
recently identified anti-GAD antibodies in serum sam- 
ples from 20 of 33 patients with stiff-man syndrome 
diagnosed at a number of institutions. The pattern of 
serum antineuronal antibody staining was unique in our

cytoplasmic and nuclear neuronal antibody labeling 
seen in control samples from patients with para- 
neoplastic syndromes.ss20 Serum from only one of over 
200 patients produced a punctate pattern suggestive of 
labeled axonal terminals, but in that patient the pattern 
of staining was clearly different from the distribution of 
GAD. 
These findings support the concept that stiff-man 
syndrome may be caused by an autoimmune mecha- 
nism.12J3,21 Solimena et all3 pointed out a high fre- 
quency of organ-specific autoimmunity in these pa- 
tients, particularly the presence of antibodies to 
pancreatic islet cells that contain GAD. Our patient had 
vitiligo, an autoimmune phenomenon present in two 
patients in the series described by Solimena et al.13 An 
anti-GAD-like autoimmune response is not present in 
all patients who present with elements of stiff-man 
syndrome. The antibody was not detected in two pa- 
tients with progressive rigidity who were later con- 
firmed not to have typical stiff-man syndrome. This 
further supports the suggestion that this antibody re- 
sponse may identify at least a subgroup of patients with 
stiff-man ~yndrome.'~ 
Antibody was not detected in the CSF from our 
patient. Solimena et all3 found that three of the 15 
patients with serum antibodies who had CSF analyzed 
did not have detectable antibody in their CSF. The 
absence of GAD-like immunoreactivity in the CSF of 
these four cases suggests that if antibody is acting at 
GABAergic terminals on motor neurons, access to these 
sites may occur from the systemic circulation. Our pa- 
tient did not have seizures, which Martinelli et alZ2 
noted in about 10% of reported cases. Twelve percent of 
patients in the series reported by Solimena et all3 had a 
history of seizures, all of them in the group that had 
autoantibodies. The presence of anti-GAD antibody in 
the CSF may place a patient at risk for seizures. 
Although our patient had marked clinical and elec- 
trophysiologic improvement concurrent with reduction 
of antibody titers during plasmapheresis, this does not 
prove that antibody causes stiff-man syndrome. Inter- 
ference with GABAergic inhibition in the spinal cord by 
anti-GAD antibody could lead to alpha motor neuron 
hyperactivity. Antibody in our patient's serum labeled 
punctate structures in the spinal cord consistent with 
GABAergic terminals on motor neurons. If anti-GAD 
antibody is etiologic for stiff-man syndrome, then anti- 
body should have access to GABAergic sites in the 
central nervous system. The original patient of Soli- 
mena et all2 had high CSF antibody titers and evidence

for intrathecal IgG synthesis, but these findings were 
not present in our patient. Alternatively, IgG can reach 
motor neurons by retrograde transport from the periph- 
Whether this route allowed access of antibody to 
GABAergic terminals in our patient is speculative. Fur- 
ther studies will be needed to determine whether the 
antibody response in these patients plays a role in the 
mechanism of rigidity, spasms, and continuous motor 
unit activity.
